strengths: Insightful critique of existing code optimization benchmarks: The paper identifies an important conceptual limitation in the PIE dataset—namely, that pairs from the same user capture mostly incremental/local optimizations rather than algorithmic innovations.
Rigorous experimental methodology: The evaluation leverages deterministic gem5 CPU simulations under GCC -O3, ensuring reliable execution time measurements and avoiding hardware/workload noise.

Comprehensive empirical investigation: The authors evaluate multiple model families (CodeLlama, DeepSeek-Coder) across different scales (7B to 34B), benchmarking both prompting strategies (Instruct, CoT) and fine-tuning variants at Best@1 and Best@8.

Effective exploration of the correctness-speedup trade-off: The paper explicitly analyzes how aggressive algorithmic rewrites degrade correctness and demonstrates that weight-space model merging (Linear and Slerp) provides a simple yet remarkably effective remedy compared to self-correction or curriculum learning.
weaknesses: Confounding factors in data construction: PIE-Problem filters pairs to those with a >90% relative time improvement and contains significantly fewer unique problems and pairs than PIE-User. It remains somewhat ambiguous whether the performance gains stem purely from cross-user diversity or from the strict speedup thresholding; an ablation separating cross-user vs. within-user at equivalent speedup thresholds would strengthen the claims.

Limited algorithmic novelty: Restructuring dataset pairs across submissions for identical competitive programming tasks is conceptually straightforward, and the model merging applied (Linear / Slerp) is off-the-shelf.

Narrow benchmark scope: Experiments are restricted to competitive programming solutions in C++ from CodeNet/PIE. While competitive programming is convenient for benchmarking algorithmic complexity, real-world software systems have modular dependencies, side effects, and readability requirements where total algorithmic redesign from raw code alone is often not directly applicable.

Absence of natural language problem specifications: The model is asked to perform optimization purely from source code without problem specifications, forcing it to reverse-engineer the intended semantics. Discussing or evaluating how problem descriptions impact correctness during global refactoring would be valuable.

strengths: Compelling and insightful motivation: The paper convincingly argues and empirically demonstrates that user-oriented iterative code refinement (as done in the PIE benchmark) primarily encourages localized, conservative edits rather than algorithmic innovation.

Rigorous evaluation methodology: Benchmarking execution times with the gem5 CPU simulator ensures deterministic, noise-free, and reproducible performance measurements on top of full compiler optimizations (-O3).
Thorough experimental setup: Evaluates multiple model architectures and scales (CodeLlama 7B/13B/34B and DeepSeek-Coder 7B/33B) under both single-sample (Best@1) and sampling (Best@8) regimes.

Effective approach to the correctness–speedup trade-off: The paper uncovers that aggressive problem-oriented optimizations degrade functional correctness, and cleverly employs model merging (weight interpolation between PIE-User and PIE-Problem models) to achieve a superior Pareto frontier compared to curriculum learning or self-correction baselines.
weaknesses: Confounding factor in dataset construction: PIE-Problem enforces a strict threshold retaining only pairs with >90% relative time improvement, whereas PIE-User uses a >10% threshold. It remains partially unclear how much of the performance gain stems from cross-programmer diversity versus simply filtering for much higher relative speedup pairs.

Discrepancy in prompting formats: PIE-User models are trained and tested using performance-conditioned prompts with score tags following Shypula et al. (2024), whereas PIE-Problem models use simple instruction prompts. A direct apple-to-apple comparison under identical prompting formats would strengthen the conclusions.

Limited task and language diversity: The evaluation is restricted to standalone C++ competitive programming problems. Real-world software optimization typically involves complex system dependencies, idiomatic libraries, and multi-file codebases, where cross-programmer global rewrites may not directly transfer.

Methodological novelty of the solution: While the problem formulation and diagnostic findings are insightful, the proposed solution primarily applies existing model merging techniques (Merge-Linear and SLERP) rather than introducing a novel algorithmic contribution for code optimization.

strengths: Compelling and intuitive problem formulation: The paper clearly identifies the limitation of existing user-centric code optimization datasets (PIE-User), where iterative edits by the same author often lead to local, incremental tweaks rather than algorithmic breakthroughs.

Rigorous evaluation methodology: Evaluating runtime using the deterministic gem5 CPU simulator alongside GCC -O3 compilation provides reproducible, non-flaky execution timing metrics, isolating true algorithmic/performance improvements beyond standard compiler optimizations.

Insightful trade-off analysis: The authors reveal a crucial dynamic—training on cross-user problem-oriented pairs (PIE-Problem) drives aggressive algorithmic optimization but harms correctness, whereas user-oriented data is conservative with high correctness.

Effective application of model merging: Applying weight merging (Merge-Linear and SLERP) between the conservative (PIE-User) and aggressive (PIE-Problem) models elegantly balances correctness and speedup, outperforming self-correction and curriculum learning baselines.
weaknesses: Semantic disconnect in cross-user pairs: Because pairs in PIE-Problem come from completely different authors with disparate coding styles, variable namings, and structural paradigms, the task risks shifting from 'optimizing existing code' to 're-implementing the problem solution from scratch'. The paper does not thoroughly analyze how much of the original program structure is preserved during inference.

Missing data mixture / multi-task baseline: The paper compares model merging against curriculum learning and self-correction, but omits a simpler and standard baseline: joint multi-task fine-tuning on a balanced mixture of PIE-User and PIE-Problem data simultaneously.

Scope and generalizability: The evaluation is limited strictly to competitive programming tasks in C++ (CodeNet/PIE). Real-world codebases involve modularity, external dependencies, and idiomatic constraints that competitive programming benchmarks do not reflect.

Heuristic filtering threshold: The 90% relative speedup cutoff used to construct PIE-Problem significantly reduces problem diversity (from 1,135 down to 336 unique problems in training), but the sensitivity to this threshold is not ablated.

strengths: The conceptual shift from user-oriented submission trajectories (PIE) to a problem-oriented perspective across multiple authors is sensible, well-motivated, and directly tackles the issue of incremental local changes versus algorithmic refactoring.

The anchor verification mechanism leverages a key property unique to code optimization—that the original 'slow code' serves as a functionally correct oracle—to produce verified input-output pairs without relying on error-prone synthetic outputs or human ground truth.

Comprehensive empirical validation across multiple open-source and proprietary models (CodeLlama, DeepSeek-Coder, Qwen2.5-Coder, GPT-4, DeepSeek-V3) demonstrates marked improvements in both speedup and optimization percentage.

The paper includes solid qualitative and quantitative analyses of the dataset shift, such as Graph Edit Distance on CFGs, embedding distribution via t-SNE, and human/LLM categorization of optimization types.
weaknesses: Test case generation in Anchor Verification relies on prompting the LLM to generate only three inputs, which can easily fail to trigger complex boundary cases or long execution paths in competitive programming problems.

The computational feasibility of executing 'slow code' as an oracle is not fully explored; very inefficient implementations on larger test inputs could suffer from Time Limit Exceeded (TLE) issues during anchor generation.
While effective, pairing submissions across users by runtime is conceptually straightforward and largely a data re-indexing strategy on the existing CodeNet/PIE corpus.

The benchmark relies on 41 competitive programming problems (978 pairs); evaluation on real-world software engineering repositories or multi-file systems is absent, limiting the assessment of generalizability to practical software development.

strengths: Novel and insightful perspective on dataset construction: The shift from user-oriented iterative trajectories (PIE) to cross-user problem-oriented trajectories (PCO) is conceptually simple yet highly effective. It allows models to learn global algorithmic transformations rather than just localized incremental refactoring.

Clever and practical verification mechanism: Leveraging the functionally correct 'slow code' as an execution anchor to produce ground-truth test outputs directly resolves the hallucination issue common in synthetic test case generation for LLM code repair.

Substantial and consistent empirical gains: Fine-tuning on PCO significantly outperforms PIE across multiple model families and sizes (CodeLlama, DeepSeek-Coder, Qwen2.5-Coder), and Anchor Verification consistently boosts correctness, optimization ratio, and speedup across GPT-4o and DeepSeek-V3 backbones.

Comprehensive empirical analyses: The paper provides informative structural (GED), semantic embedding, human/LLM categorization, and data-efficiency scaling analyses, supported by clear qualitative case studies in the appendix.
weaknesses: Evaluation scope is restricted to competitive programming: The dataset is derived solely from CodeNet/PIE. While standard in this line of work, competitive programming benchmarks rely on standalone programs with clean standard I/O; evaluating how this generalizes to real-world software engineering repositories with external dependencies and multi-file structures remains open.

Lack of details regarding timeout handling in Anchor Verification: The slow code is functionally correct but computationally inefficient. The paper does not thoroughly discuss how timeout limits or potential TLEs (Time Limit Exceeded) are handled when executing the slow anchor code on LLM-generated boundary/stress test inputs.

Unquantified runtime and token overhead: The multi-stage Anchor Verification process introduces extra LLM calls (explaining code, generating test inputs, and iterative repair) and compilation/execution cycles. Reporting the runtime latency and computational/token costs compared to single-pass baseline generation would provide a more complete picture of practical trade-offs.

Clarification needed on trajectory sampling: The paper mentions selecting pairs with the top speedup rankings to match the sample count of PIE (78K pairs), but more formal detail on how pairs are sampled across the full chain of submissions would improve clarity and reproducibility.

strengths: Insightful problem reformulation: Shifting from user-oriented (same-user iterative submissions) to problem-oriented (cross-user submissions) optimization pairs is well-motivated. It effectively breaks the cognitive inertia of single-developer edits, exposing models to diverse algorithmic strategies rather than minor constant-factor or syntax tweaks.

Comprehensive empirical and qualitative analyses: The authors provide compelling structural (Graph Edit Distance on CFGs), semantic (code embedding t-SNE), and qualitative (human and LLM categorization of global vs. local optimizations) analyses to demonstrate why problem-oriented pairs differ fundamentally from user-oriented ones.

Well-tailored Anchor Verification mechanism: Exploiting the fact that the original 'slow code' is already functionally correct as an execution oracle for generated test inputs is an elegant and effective adaptation of differential testing for LLM self-refinement, successfully mitigating the correctness penalty ('optimization tax').

Strong and consistent experimental gains: Substantial improvements are demonstrated across multiple modern Code LLMs (e.g., Qwen2.5-Coder, DeepSeek-Coder, CodeLlama, GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3), with significant boosts in both %OPT and runtime speedup under rigorous CPU simulation (gem5).
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is somewhat incremental: The problem-oriented approach is essentially a re-pairing strategy over existing competitive programming data (CodeNet / PIE), and anchor verification is an application of differential testing / dual-execution oracle to prompt-based repair.

Scope limited to competitive programming: The evaluation and dataset construction rely exclusively on competitive programming submissions (CodeNet/PIE). In practical software engineering, code optimization involves complex system dependencies, architectural constraints, and API contracts, where complete algorithmic rewrites across unrelated implementations may not directly transfer.

Handling of corner cases and timeouts in Anchor Verification: The paper uses only 3 test inputs generated by the LLM, which may have limited coverage on edge cases. Furthermore, the paper does not clearly discuss how timeouts are handled when executing the 'slow code' on large or worst-case generated inputs during test case construction.

Semantic equivalence risks: Cross-user submissions may satisfy the test suite of a contest platform but could have subtle differences in formatting, handling of ill-formed inputs, or undefined behavior. The paper does not thoroughly discuss filtering protocols for ensuring strict semantic equivalence across different users' solutions.

strengths: The core conceptual insight—shifting from user-oriented submission trajectories (PIE) to problem-oriented trajectories (PCO)—is intuitive, elegant, and directly addresses the tendency of LLMs to stick to local/incremental edits rather than exploring algorithmic rewrites.

The Anchor Verification Framework leverages a unique and natural property of code optimization (the existence of an inefficient yet functionally correct reference code) to generate ground-truth test inputs and outputs, effectively addressing the 'optimization tax' (correctness degradation).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across diverse open-source and proprietary models (Qwen2.5-Coder, DeepSeek-Coder, CodeLlama, GPT-4/4o), showing consistent and substantial gains in speedup, percentage optimized (%OPT), and correctness.

Thorough analysis and ablations, including disentangling perspective vs. selection effects (PCO-Random vs. PCO-Top-Speedup), structural analysis (GED), physical hardware validation confirming gem5 simulation trends, and cross-language validation on Python.
weaknesses: The evaluation is restricted to competitive programming benchmarks (CodeNet/PIE tasks). Practical enterprise codebases often feature complex dependencies, global states, and APIs that make isolated execution and synthetic input generation significantly more difficult.

A potential limitation of the Anchor Verification Framework is that generating large or worst-case inputs for the 'slow code' could lead to execution timeouts, while small inputs may fail to trigger subtle edge-case bugs in the optimized solution.
Pairing arbitrary user submissions from the same problem can occasionally introduce differences in input/output parsing or variable conventions, which may act as confounding factors during training.

strengths: Conceptual insight and paradigm shift: The transition from a user-oriented perspective (iterative submissions from the same user, which are typically incremental or local) to a problem-oriented perspective (aggregating submissions across diverse users for the same problem) is conceptually simple yet highly effective. It enables models to learn genuine algorithmic shifts rather than superficial tweaks.

Clever domain-specific verification mechanism: The Anchor Verification Framework smartly exploits an asymmetry unique to program optimization—namely, that the input code is inefficient but functionally correct. Using the slow code as an execution oracle for LLM-generated test inputs provides reliable, verified test suites without human labeling or error-prone synthetic assertions.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The paper conducts thorough experiments across multiple model families (CodeLlama, DeepSeekCoder, Qwen2.5-Coder) and scales (7B to 33B), comparing against strong prompting baselines (Instruct, CoT) and alternate refinement methods (Self-Debugging, Direct Test Generation).

Rigorous ablations and analyses: The manuscript includes several commendable analyses, such as disentangling the perspective shift from speedup-selection bias (Appendix H), investigating structural disparities using Graph Edit Distance (GED), validating gem5 simulator results against physical Xeon server hardware, and extending experiments to Python.
weaknesses: Limitation of benchmark domain: The evaluation is conducted entirely on competitive programming problems (CodeNet/PIE benchmark). These tasks typically feature pure algorithmic logic with simple stdin/stdout interfaces. In real-world software engineering, code optimization involves complex object state, external dependencies, database access, and concurrency, where treating the legacy code as a black-box test anchor is significantly more difficult.

Oracle execution cost for slow code: When the baseline code suffers from severe asymptotic inefficiency (e.g., exponential or factorial time complexity), running it as an execution oracle on arbitrary inputs risks timeouts or severe overhead. While the authors discuss time limits and input truncation in the appendix, a more systematic mechanism for bounding input scale during anchor execution is desirable.

Test suite adequacy and false positives: The anchor verification relies on generating 3 test inputs. If the LLM generates overly simple or non-discriminating inputs, semantically incorrect optimizations may pass the test suite and introduce silent regressions, which relates directly to why roughly half of the remaining failures are 'compiled, semantic wrong'.

strengths: Clear, intuitive, and well-motivated core ideas: restructuring optimization pairs across different users (problem-oriented perspective) naturally encourages LLMs to learn global algorithmic transformations rather than incremental localized edits.

The Anchor Verification Framework effectively exploits a unique property of code optimization—that the original code is functional/correct—to create verified test suites (via execution) without ground-truth unit tests, successfully mitigating semantic drift ('optimization tax').

Thorough and rigorous experimental validation: the paper evaluates across diverse model families (Qwen2.5-Coder, DeepSeek-Coder, CodeLlama, GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3), utilizes the gem5 cycle-accurate simulator with GCC -O3 flags, and validates performance on physical hardware (Intel Xeon Platinum).

Strong set of ablation studies, including isolating perspective shift from selection bias (PCO-Random vs. PCO-Top-Speedup), Graph Edit Distance stratification, data scaling curves, and cross-language evaluation on Python.
weaknesses: The evaluation is restricted to competitive programming tasks (CodeNet/PIE). Real-world software performance engineering involves large codebases, multi-threading, complex API interactions, memory hierarchy management, and distributed systems, which limits immediate applicability to broader software engineering settings.

Risk of benchmark contamination: CodeNet problems and standard competitive programming algorithms are likely represented in the pretraining corpora of frontier models (e.g., GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3, Qwen2.5-Coder). While test splits are problem-disjoint, pretraining exposure could inflate performance on algorithmic shifts.

Handling pathological inputs for slow code: If the initial code has high complexity (e.g., exponential or factorial) on certain edge cases, executing LLM-generated inputs could trigger severe execution timeouts or resource exhaustion. While timeout mechanisms are mentioned in Appendix L, a more comprehensive empirical study on timeout rates and input constraint handling would strengthen the anchor verification pipeline.

Conflation of correctness and speedup metrics: Assigning 1.0x speedup to incorrect outputs (following PIE) means that raw speedup gains are mathematically coupled with correctness improvements, making it slightly harder to isolate pure execution latency improvements on solely correct programs.
